source_text: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ· λέγεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος αὐτόχθων. τούτων δὲ ἄλλαιν δυοῖν νεώτερα τὰ Φθιωτικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Δευκαλίωνος. εἰς δὲ τὸν χρόνον τῶν Τρωϊκῶν ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου γενεαὶ μὲν εἴκοσι ἢ μιᾷ πλείους διαριθμοῦνται, ἔτη δέ, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, τετρακόσια καὶ πρόσω. εἰ δὲ τὰ Ἀσσυρίων πολλοῖς ἔτεσι πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἀφ’ ὧν Κτησίας λέγει, φανήσεται τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ ἔτει τῆς Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχῆς, τῆς δὲ Βηλούχου τοῦ ὀγδόου δυναστείας τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἡ Μωυσέως κατὰ Ἄμωσιν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον καὶ κατὰ Ἴναχον τὸν Ἀργεῖον ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κίνησις. ἦν δὲ κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα κατὰ μὲν Φορωνέα τὸν μετὰ Ἴναχον ὁ ἐπὶ Ὠγύγου κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἡ ἐν Σικυῶνι βασιλεία, πρώτου μὲν Αἰγιαλέως, εἶτα Εὔρωπος, εἶτα Τελχῖνος, καὶ ἡ Κρητὸς ἐν Κρήτῃ.
pass_a_gloss: And concerning the fact that the doctrines of the philosophers were seen among the Hebrews, we will speak a little later, but first, as was fitting, we must speak about the times of Moses, through which it will be shown clearly that the philosophy among the Hebrews is the most ancient of all wisdom. For Tatian has spoken precisely about these things in his work Against the Greeks, and also Cassian has spoken in the first of his Exegetical works; however, the memorandum also demands that we run through the things said according to the place. Apion the grammarian, also called Plistonicus, in the fourth of his Egyptian histories, although he is disposed in a hostile manner towards the Hebrews, being an Egyptian by race, and having even written a book against the Jews, mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events that occurred during his reign, and presents Ptolemy of Mendes as a witness. And the words of the latter are as follows: Amosis, having become king in the place of Argive Inachus, dug up Auaria, as Ptolemy of Mendes wrote in his Chronicles. This Ptolemy was a priest, and having set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three whole books, says that during the reign of Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews, led by Moses, made their journey out of Egypt, from which it is inferred that Moses flourished during the time of Inachus. But the most ancient of the Greek things are the Argolic, which I call the things from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles; and of these, the Attic, which are from Cecrops, the two-natured and autochthonous, as Tatian says word for word, are forty generations younger; and the Arcadic, which are from Pelasgus, are nine; and this one is also said to be autochthonous. And of these, the Phthiotic, which are from Deucalion, are two generations younger. And into the time of the Trojan War, twenty generations or a little more are reckoned from Inachus, and, so to speak, four hundred years. But if the things of the Assyrians are much older than the Greek things, as Ctesias says, it will be shown that in the second and four hundredth year of the Assyrian reign, and in the second and thirtieth year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus, the movement of Moses out of Egypt, during the reign of Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive, occurred. And in Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who was after Inachus, there was the flood that occurred in the time of Ogygus, and the kingdom in Sicyon, first of Aegialeus, then of Eurypus, then of Telchin, and the kingdom of Crete in Crete.
pass_b_english: We will address the claim that Greek philosophical doctrines were found among the Hebrews a little later. First, as the logical order requires, we must discuss the era of Moses, because it will demonstrate conclusively that Hebrew philosophy is the oldest of all wisdom. Tatian has already treated these matters precisely in his *Address to the Greeks*, and Cassian has done so in the first book of his *Exegetical Works*; nevertheless, this memorandum obliges us to summarize the relevant points again.

Consider the testimony of Apion the grammarian, surnamed Plistonicus. In the fourth book of his *Egyptian History*, he adopts a hostile attitude toward the Hebrews—he is Egyptian by birth and even composed a treatise against the Jews—yet he cites Amosis, an Egyptian king, and the events of his reign, and he calls Ptolemy of Mendes as a witness. Ptolemy's own words run as follows: "Amosis, who became king in the time of the Argive Inachus, razed Avaris," just as Ptolemy of Mendes recorded in his *Chronicles*.

This Ptolemy was a priest. After setting out the deeds of the Egyptian kings in three complete books, he states that during the reign of Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews made their exodus from Egypt under the leadership of Moses. From this it follows that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus.

The Argolic traditions, which stem from Inachus, are the most ancient in Greece, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his *Chronicles*. Compared with them, the Attic line from Cecrops—who was two-natured and autochthonous, to use Tatian's exact phrase—is forty generations younger; the Arcadian line from Pelasgus—also said to be autochthonous—is nine generations younger; and the Phthiotic line from Deucalion is two generations younger still. Up to the era of the Trojan War, one counts roughly twenty generations from Inachus, amounting, so to speak, to four hundred years.

If, as Ctesias asserts, Assyrian history is many years older than Greek history, then the exodus of Moses from Egypt under the Egyptian Amosis and the Argive Inachus falls in the 402nd year of the Assyrian empire and the 32nd year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus. Meanwhile in Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, Inachus' successor, the flood of Ogygus occurred and the kingdom of Sicyon began—first under Aegialeus, then Eurypus, then Telchin—and the kingdom of Crete was established in Crete.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex chronological arguments and historical citations. Pass A preserves the nuances of the Greek (e.g., 'disposed in a hostile manner' for 'φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος'), and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that maintains the same meaning without adding or contradicting the source. The distinction between the different Greek lineages (Argolic, Attic, Arcadic, Phthiotic) and their respective generational distances is correctly rendered in both.
